titleStmt.title: Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State

div.head: 480. Telegram From Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation to the Department of State
div.p: Secto 19061. Subject: Secretary’s Bilateral with President Lusinchi October 1.

2. Summary. In a lengthy conversation with Secretary Shultz October 1, Venezuelan President Lusinchi gave assurances that his government is not deceived by the Nicaraguans but has rather consistently warned GON leaders against interfering in their neighbors’ affairs. The Secretary reviewed US views on a final Contadora agreement and pointed out the Core Four’s objections to Contadora’s recent report to the UNSYG. The Secretary gave Lusinchi advance notice of the possible meeting with Ortega and the upcoming meeting with the Soviets. Discussion of the current COM vacancy in Caracas is reported septel. End of summary.

3. Secretary met morning October 1 with Venezuelan President Lusinchi in his suite at the St. Regis Hotel, New York. FonMin Consalvi and Ambassador to the US Valentin Hernandez were most prominent among the many Venezuelans present. Others on US side were A/Sec Elliott Abrams, Spokesman Bernard Kalb, Stephanie von Reigersberg (interpreter) and ARA/AND Phil McLean (notetaker).

4. Lusinchi began with personal compliments for the Secretary’s skills. He then delivered a lengthy exposition of Venezuelan views on Central America. He said the Venezuelan position is to promote dialogue and achieve democratic solutions in each of the Central American States. Pursuing that peace has been the GOV’s main activity at this UNGA. In a region easily influenced by outside forces, the Nicaraguans are acting as Soviet pawns. The kidnapping of President Duarte’s daughter is an idiocy which postpones any possibility of making progress on peace in El Salvador and may lead the guerrillas into a final confrontation. Until intelligence confirmed the leftists’ role, the GOV suspected it was a rightist provocation. The GOV is
contacting UNGO and others to see what it can do. The situation in Costa Rica is also dangerous. At least in Guatemala the crisis is easing. Mejia is acting reasonably and, he noted with pleasure, the US is encouraging progress. He cautioned the US not to overemphasize the region’s “negative factors”, apparently a reference to the Contras who he claimed are ineffective because of their ties to the Somozistas.

5. The Secretary began his reply by noting our appreciation of Venezuela’s candid and realistic appraisals. The US supports Contadora and wants to see it come to a positive conclusion, but because of the track record of communist governments the agreement must include simultaneity, verification and a schedule of provisions for national reconciliation. Without these elements, any agreement would not bind the Nicaraguans at all. On the other hand, if the US undertakes to stop aid, it will stop aid. The decrease in US influence would leave the communists in the driver’s seat. The Secretary said he had just talked to the four Central American Foreign Ministers who say they will challenge an inaccurate and biased report they say the Contadora countries are going to submit to the UNSYG.

6. FonMin replied that none of the countries have indicated displeasure to the GOV, though there had been meetings with two of them just that day. The report, already submitted to the UNSYG, is a simple recounting of the Contadora process up to this point without any evaluation or intention to favor any side. It does outline the three issues which remain to be resolved, i.e. armaments, follow-up on security systems and reconciliation. Lusinchi interjected to assure the Secretary that the GOV consistently tells the Nicaraguans there is no role from them in solving their neighbors’ problems, either by invoking “revolutionary solidarity” with the Salvadorean rebels or supporting “autonomous groups” in Costa Rica.

7. The Secretary concluded by raising three topics briefly. First, the GOV may hear that Amb. Schlaudeman will be meeting with Ortega. The purpose will be to say the Manzanillo talks can only be re-started if a national dialogue under church sponsorship is underway. Second,
later this month A/Sec Abrams will be meeting with the Soviets to discuss Central America and the Caribbean. The purpose is to tell the Soviets that their activities in the region are unwelcome and unwarranted. The GOV should know the US will make no deals with the Soviets. Third, Puerto Rico is not a colony. The only difference among the Puerto Rican people is whether they should seek statehood or remain with their present status. This subject has no place in the UN as a decolonization subject. The Venezuelans gave no reaction to these last points.
8. At the conclusion of the discussion the Secretary raised the current COM vacancy in Caracas. That discussion is reported septel.
9. Department please pass to Caracas, San Salvador, Managua, Guatemala, San Jose and Tegucigalpa.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, [no n number]. Secret; Immediate; Nodis.

In an October 1 memorandum to Reagan, Shultz wrote: “Venezuelan President Lusinchi assured me today that his government is not deceived by the Sandinistas and will not tolerate their interference in Costa Rican or Salvadoran affairs. The Venezuelans are doing what they can with their Salvadoran guerrilla contacts to encourage the release of Duarte’s daughter. Lusinchi heard me out as I conveyed your support for Otto Reich’s nomination to be our next Ambassador in Caracas. He told us of his predecessor’s bad experience with President Kennedy’s Ambassador, Teodoro Moscoso, a person who seemed to have badly rankled the Venezuelans. In the end, Lusinchi said the AFL-CIO had now recommended Otto’s qualifications, and in view of our traditional friendship, his government will agree to the nomination when his name is submitted.” (Reagan Library, Executive Secretariat, NSC Records, System File, System II, Case 91018)
Reference is to telegram Secto 19058 from Secretary of State Shultz’s Delegation, October 2. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, [no film number])
